sections.heading: How We Rank Build and Kill Zombies Parts and Skills
paragraphs: Rankings weigh four things: whether the upgrade is permanent, whether the car can function without it, how much it extends run distance, and how early it starts paying off. A part that the car cannot leave the spawn without beats a part that only shines late, and anything permanent outranks anything replaceable.

The game does not publish exact stats for every part, so this Build and Kill Zombies tier list deliberately ranks by role and timing rather than pretending at numbers that nobody can verify. When updates shuffle the machines, the ranking gets re-reviewed against how the new parts actually behave.

sections.heading: S Tier: Highest-Priority Upgrades
sections.intro: S tier is where Cash goes first. These three decide whether a run works at all.

subsections.heading: Fuel for the target run
paragraphs: Distance is the scoreboard in Build and Kill Zombies, and the tank is the leash. Fuel that matches the run you are attempting turns every other upgrade into usable value; a monster engine with a tiny tank just changes where you strand yourself. Match the tank to the route before upgrading anything flashy.

subsections.heading: Engine that can move the current chassis
paragraphs: The engine's job is to haul whatever you have bolted together. As Blocks accumulate and the chassis grows, an engine that was fine yesterday starts struggling. Upgrade the engine when weight goes up, not because a bigger number exists.

subsections.heading: Early permanent Luck progression
paragraphs: Luck is a Skill, which means it stays on the account while parts come and go. Investing in Luck early improves every future roll from the CAR PARTS and SUPPORTS machines, which compounds quietly across the whole life of the account. Few purchases in the game keep paying that long.

sections.heading: A Tier: Strong Next Upgrades
sections.intro: A tier turns a functional car into a profitable one.

subsections.heading: Wheels and chassis balance
paragraphs: Speed means nothing if the car tips, drifts into hordes, or crawls up slopes. Wheels and chassis layout are the difference between a fast car and a controllable one, and controllable cars drive further. If the car feels unstable at speed, this is the fix.

subsections.heading: A reliable Support or weapon
paragraphs: Kills pay. A car that runs the whole map but kills nothing collects distance rewards and leaves the rest behind. One dependable Support, placed where it can actually reach zombies, converts driving time into Cash at a much better rate.

subsections.heading: More Support when extra weapons actually help
paragraphs: More Support raises support capacity, which only matters once you have supports worth carrying. It is a strong purchase for mature builds running multiple weapons, and a wasted one for a car still deciding on its first.

sections.heading: B Tier and Late-Game Choices
paragraphs: B tier is timing, not quality. Gold Roll and other premium progression options cost more than early accounts can spare, but they compress the grind once the cheap upgrades are done. Situational extra parts from the CAR PARTS machine, niche wheels, spare Fuels, and heavier Blocks, belong here too: useful in the right build, dead Cash in the wrong one.
The test for any B tier purchase is simple: name the run where it pays for itself. If the answer is vague, the S and A tier rows above are still the better home for your Cash.

faq.question: What is the best thing to upgrade first in Build and Kill Zombies?
faq.answer: Fuel and an engine that can move your chassis, in whatever order your current build is weakest. Distance ends when the tank or the engine gives out, so those two sit at the top of the tier list, with early Luck close behind because it is permanent.

faq.question: Are Skills better than car parts?
faq.answer: They are different: parts make the current car work, Skills make every future roll and run better. Luck, More Support, and Gold Roll are permanent, so once the car can run, putting early Cash into Luck usually outearns another replaceable part.

faq.question: When should I roll the SUPPORTS machine?
faq.answer: As soon as your car can drive a full route, because supports are how driving turns into kills and Cash. Roll the CAR PARTS machine first only if the car cannot yet run reliably.

faq.question: Is Gold Roll worth it?
faq.answer: For late-game accounts with Cash to spare, premium rolls like Gold Roll compress the grind. For new players it is a B tier purchase: the cheaper permanent upgrades, especially Luck, deliver more per Cash spent.

hero.heading: Build and Kill Zombies Best Build
hero.lead: The Build and Kill Zombies best build is a working chain, not one part: an Engine that can move your chassis, Fuel matched to the run, stable Wheels, a Support placed to actually hit zombies, and permanent Skills improving every roll behind it.

sections.heading: Best Starter Car Build
paragraphs: The tutorial hands you the pieces of a first car, and the starter build is about finishing that loop cleanly rather than optimizing. Get an engine mounted, attach a fuel tank, put wheels on the chassis, and add the first Support. That is a complete car: it runs, it burns fuel over distance, and it kills.

Resist upgrading any single slot to maximum during the tutorial phase. The starter loop exists to teach the build area and earn your first Cash and Studs, and a balanced starter car earns faster than a lopsided one that dies or strands early. Save the deep upgrades for the setup order below.

sections.heading: Engine and Fuel: Make the Build Actually Run
paragraphs: Engine and Fuel are a pair, and the Build and Kill Zombies best build always treats them as one decision. The engine has to move the chassis you have actually assembled, and Blocks are heavy: a car that grew three pieces heavier needs engine attention even if nothing else changed. An underpowered engine shows up as sluggish acceleration and hills you cannot climb.

Fuel is the leash on the whole run. Distance, which is what pays Studs, ends when the tank does, so a tank that runs dry halfway to your target wastes everything mounted behind it. The practical rule: size the tank for the route, then make the engine capable of hauling the weight over that route. When either changes, re-check the other.

sections.heading: Wheels, Blocks and Chassis Layout
paragraphs: Blocks are the body of the car, and how they spread weight matters as much as how many you have. A tall, top-heavy chassis tips; a long, flat one tracks straight and survives contact with hordes better. Wheels carry that layout: enough of them to bear the weight, positioned so the car does not sag at one end.

The symptom of a layout problem is easy to spot: the car drifts when it should turn straight, or dips and scrapes when it leaves the spawn area. Fix layout with wheel placement and Block redistribution before buying power, because extra engine force on an unstable chassis just makes the crashes faster.

sections.heading: Best SUPPORTS and Weapon Placement
paragraphs: The SUPPORTS machine rolls weapons and add-ons that are separate from the CAR PARTS machine, and the distinction matters: parts make the car run, supports make it kill. Kills are what turn distance into full Cash rewards, so a car that runs beautifully but carries no real support is earning a fraction of what it could.

Placement decides whether a support earns its slot. Weapons that cover one side leave the other side free for zombies, and rear coverage matters more than most players expect. Spread coverage so the car has an answer from every angle, and remember that More Support, the Skill, expands how much you can carry once the first weapons are already pulling their weight.

sections.heading: Skills for a Better Long-Term Build
paragraphs: Skills are the account-level layer of the Build and Kill Zombies best build. Luck improves what the machines give you, which quietly upgrades every CAR PARTS and SUPPORTS roll for the rest of the account's life. More Support expands carrying capacity, and Gold Roll is a premium progression option for accounts that have outgrown the cheap upgrades.

The reason Skills rank so high for a long-term build is simple: parts are replaceable, Skills are not. Every Cash point into Luck keeps paying after the car it was earned with has been scrapped and rebuilt twice. Start with Luck early, add More Support when your weapon loadout justifies it, and leave Gold Roll until the rest of the account is mature.

steps.heading: Survives but kills poorly

steps.heading: Rolls keep disappointing
steps.description: Skills. Luck upgrades every future CAR PARTS and SUPPORTS roll, which is the account-level fix.

sections.heading: Common Build Mistakes
bullets: Maxing one slot while another sits empty, usually a huge engine on a three-wheel chassis.
Ignoring fuel size, then blaming difficulty for runs that end because the tank ran dry.
Stacking all weapons on one side, leaving a blind zone zombies learn about before you do.
Rolling SUPPORTS before the car can complete a route, buying weapons for a car that cannot drive.
Spending every Cash point on replaceable parts while permanent Skills like Luck stay untouched.

sections.heading: Best Build for Longer Runs
paragraphs: Long runs multiply everything: distance pays more Studs, but fuel burns longer and one layout flaw ends the trip. The build answer is the same chain, scaled up: bigger tank matched by a bigger engine, a chassis that stays stable at the new weight, and support coverage that can handle sustained contact.
Boss timers complicate long runs, because the countdown does not care how far from spawn you are. Before pushing distance, read the boss guide so the run does not end at the worst possible moment.

sections.heading: How Build and Kill Zombies Works
paragraphs: Build and Kill Zombies runs a loop with two halves. In the base area, machines and the build area: the CAR PARTS machine rolls Blocks, Engines, Wheels, and Fuels, the SUPPORTS machine rolls weapons and add-ons, and Cash pays for it all. Out on the road, the driving half: distance and kills earn Cash and Studs, and Studs track your best distance, which some code rewards check.

The two halves feed each other. A better car drives further and kills more, which earns more Cash, which buys better rolls. Skills like Luck sit above the loop permanently, improving what the machines hand out.

sections.heading: How to Roll CAR PARTS and SUPPORTS
paragraphs: The CAR PARTS machine is the physical car: Blocks form the chassis, the Engine moves it, the fuel Tank feeds it, and Wheels carry it. Early rolls should aim for the minimum drivable set, engine plus tank plus wheels, before chasing anything bigger.

The SUPPORTS machine is a separate roll pool for weapons and add-ons. New players often skip it and discover a car that drives the whole map while killing nothing, which pays poorly. One early support roll, one usable weapon, is enough to double the value of the same distance.
Luck, the Skill, improves what both machines give you over time, which is why a small early investment in it keeps paying long after the current car is scrapped.

sections.heading: How to Drive and Earn Cash
paragraphs: Driving is where the loop pays. Distance builds Studs, kills and progress pay Cash, and both feed the machines back at base. The habit that matters most early is completing routes: a moderate run that ends on purpose with a working car earns more over an evening than record attempts that keep wrecking.

Push distance in steps. When a route ends because the tank ran dry, fuel is the upgrade. When it ends because zombies stopped the car, supports and layout are. Letting each failed run point at its bottleneck is the whole skill of the game, and it works from the very first drive.

sections.heading: Build and Kill Zombies Controls
paragraphs: Driving and movement follow the on-screen prompts in the current game interface, so check the control hints shown during your first session rather than memorizing a fixed key list. Building and rolling happen through the on-screen machine and build menus rather than hidden hotkeys, and Roblox games can remap individual keys per update, so the in-game settings and controls panel is always the reliable reference.

Nothing in the core loop requires memorized shortcuts: rolling parts, assembling the car, and driving are all handled through the visible interfaces, which is why the first-10-minutes route above works without a key list.

After those four jobs are covered, put Cash into Luck, the Skill that improves every future roll from both machines.

faq.answer: Complete routes with a car that can both drive and kill. Distance pays Studs and kills pay Cash, so one working support on a car that finishes its route outearns a faster car that wrecks halfway.

faq.question: What are CAR PARTS and SUPPORTS?
faq.answer: CAR PARTS rolls the physical pieces, Blocks, Engines, Wheels, and Fuels. SUPPORTS rolls weapons and add-ons from a separate machine. A working build needs both: parts so the car runs, supports so it kills.

hero.heading: Build and Kill Zombies Boss Guide
hero.lead: This Build and Kill Zombies boss guide covers the NEXT BOSS IN countdown, what to fix before it reaches zero, and the build priorities that keep a car alive when the boss arrives.

sections.heading: Build and Kill Zombies Boss Guide: Quick Answer
paragraphs: NEXT BOSS IN is the countdown the HUD shows before a boss encounter, and it is the game's own signal for when to stop pushing distance and start preparing. Use the window to check your Engine and Fuel against the current chassis, confirm SUPPORTS coverage, and spend Cash on rolls or upgrades while it is still safe to drive. The sections below cover how to read the timer, what the current Zeus Event adds, and which build priorities matter before a boss run.

sections.heading: How the Build and Kill Zombies Boss Timer Works
paragraphs: NEXT BOSS IN is displayed in the HUD during play, counting down to the next boss encounter. The safe way to use it is as your personal schedule: farm early in the window while the risk is low, then stop pushing distance as the clock runs down, so the final minutes go to preparation instead of one more risky route.

The exact spawn behavior, where the boss appears and whether timers pause between runs, is the kind of detail that changes with updates. The reliable part is the countdown itself: it is visible, it is the game's own signal, and every preparation decision should be measured against it.

sections.heading: Zeus Event and Zeus Boss Fight
paragraphs: Update 3 brought the Zeus Event, the game's current limited-time event, with a Zeus Boss Fight as its headline content. The event adds Lightning Tokens as its own currency, and the ZEUS code redeems for 50 of them, which makes that code the fastest free entry into the event's rewards.

Public event tracking has shown the Zeus Event window running into early October 2026, but event end dates shift with updates, so check the official Roblox game page for the current status before planning around it. Boss specifics like exact health or attack patterns are not published by the developer, and this guide sticks to what is confirmed rather than inventing numbers.

sections.heading: What to Do Before NEXT BOSS IN Reaches Zero
paragraphs: Run this checklist in order while the countdown is still comfortable.
bullets: Confirm the engine can still move the current chassis weight before the encounter starts.
Check the fuel tank against the routes you actually drive, so a short tank does not cut a session short.
Reposition weapons so coverage reaches every side of the car, not just the front.
Bank early: roll and spend Cash before the final stretch so nothing important is left half-bought.
Compare your current setup against the tier list and buy the weakest link while there is still time to test it.

sections.heading: Best Build Priorities for Boss Runs
paragraphs: Boss encounters reward preparation more than any single part. Engine and Fuel come first, because the car has to complete routes while carrying every upgrade you have bolted on. After that, SUPPORTS coverage does the heavy lifting: weapons that hit reliably from the placement you can actually build are worth more than one oversized roll in the wrong slot, and a chassis and wheel layout that stays stable at full weight keeps the whole setup working.

Skills stay valuable here too: Luck improves the rolls that upgrade everything else before the fight, not during it. The best build page holds the full setup chain, and the tier list ranks exactly which upgrade closes which gap.

sections.heading: Common Boss Run Mistakes
bullets: Rolling new parts minutes before the encounter and never testing whether the car still runs.
Leaving Cash unspent during the window, then facing the boss with upgrades still on the board.
Covering only one side of the car with weapons while the other angles stay open.
Skipping the fuel check, so the run ends because the tank ran dry rather than in the fight.
Spending the entire preparation window on risky distance attempts instead of finishing the build.

sections.heading: Keep Improving Your Boss Odds
paragraphs: Boss preparation is build preparation done early. The beginner guide covers the fundamentals if the loop itself still feels shaky, and the wiki home keeps every guide and the current codes one click away.

faq.question: How does the boss timer work?
faq.answer: The HUD shows NEXT BOSS IN, a visible countdown to the next boss encounter. Treat it as your preparation schedule: farm early in the window, then spend the final stretch rolling, upgrading, and testing the build before it reaches zero.

faq.question: What is the current boss event?
faq.answer: The Zeus Event from Update 3 is the current limited-time event, featuring the Zeus Boss Fight and Lightning Tokens as event currency. Event windows shift with updates, so confirm the live status on the official Roblox game page.

faq.question: What should I upgrade before a boss?
faq.answer: Whatever the chain is missing: engine power for the current chassis weight, fuel for the routes you drive, support coverage on every side, and any upgrade rolls still sitting unspent. The tier list ranks these systems in order.

faq.question: What should I do when NEXT BOSS IN is low?
faq.answer: Stop pushing for distance and use what is left of the window to prepare: spend accumulated Cash on rolls or upgrades, check that the engine still moves the chassis and the tank covers your route, and confirm weapon placement covers the car. The countdown is the game's own signal, so planning against it is the whole skill.

steps.heading: Make a short drive

steps.heading: Add one weapon role
steps.description: Choose one exposed contact mount or one ranged weapon with a clear firing direction. Confirm placement and support capacity in your own builder rather than copying the number of mounts in a sketch.

subsections.heading: The new loadout earns less
paragraphs: Compare fuel, travel and weapon contact separately. A new mount may have hidden the old weapon behind the chassis, or the car may simply be less manageable. faq.answer: Use the compact starter. A small connected frame with a seat, engine, fuel and balanced wheels makes failures easy to diagnose. Add a weapon once it drives reliably, then adapt the hybrid sketch.

faq.answer: Choose space for a specific part or mounting job. A longer central area can accommodate fuel, while a wider platform can separate mounts. Test handling after changing either dimension.

faq.question: Can I use Fast Furious or Blue Monster instead?

sections.heading: Fit the weapon to the car

subsections.heading: Contact loadouts
paragraphs: Begin with a front attachment point that the chassis does not hide. Drive toward a comparable group and watch whether the working surface meets zombies before the body does. If a weapon sits too high or behind the frame, move it before changing the rest of the car.

A compact starter or hybrid is a useful test bed because there is less surrounding construction to inspect. Keep the old mount position in mind, or take your own screenshot, so you can undo an experiment that performs worse. Treat front placement as a starting test, not a universal rule for every item.

subsections.heading: Ranged loadouts
paragraphs: A Crossbow needs a useful view toward approaching enemies. Check the direction of the mounted piece and whether blocks or other equipment sit ahead of it. Turn the car during a test and compare what happens when a target is in front of the weapon versus off to one side.

A ranged mount is an option when you want a different engagement position from the contact weapon. It does not justify covering every spare surface. Verify one mount first, then add complementary equipment only when the extra capacity and the physical layout allow it.

subsections.heading: Capacity and ownership
paragraphs: Watch the builder support counter while equipping each piece. More Support skills expand support capacity, but the live counter is the useful answer for the item you are placing. Do not assume every object in the weapons inventory consumes the same kind of slot.

An empty slot is not missing damage if you have nothing suitable to place in it. A weapon in inventory also contributes nothing until it is fitted. Check ownership, placement acceptance and the support count before purchasing another capacity upgrade.

paragraphs: Skills are purchased upgrades separate from the replaceable parts you fit to a vehicle. The SKILLS interface contains connected upgrade branches, so skill tree is an appropriate description of its layout. Read the path and prerequisites shown in your current interface before planning a purchase several nodes away.

The three lines below answer different needs. Their names are useful even when a guide does not carry a complete price list: roll quality, equipment capacity and access to gold-roll progression. Costs and higher-rank details should come from the tooltip in the current game.

sections.heading: Choose your next upgrade by your current session

subsections.heading: New player: establish a working loop
paragraphs: First make sure the vehicle can drive. A skill purchase does not install an engine or supply an empty fuel tank. Keep enough Cash to address a missing movement part and get through another ordinary run, then inspect the first affordable Luck option.

Luck is a sensible early preference when you will make many more rolls. Its benefit concerns later equipment opportunities; it is not a direct repair for poor steering or a misplaced weapon. Take the cheaper useful step you can actually unlock rather than saving blindly for a distant node.

subsections.heading: Cash-focused session: improve future purchases
paragraphs: For a session built around repeated drives, identify whether your problem is the vehicle or the next series of rolls. If the car repeatedly stops because of fuel, a practical part purchase may help the next run more immediately than another skill. If the car is dependable and new equipment is the next goal, review Luck.

Use More Support when the limit is the obstacle. A spare slot with no suitable item is an investment waiting for inventory; a blocked second useful mount has an immediate use. Compare these situations before treating support capacity as a compulsory second purchase.

subsections.heading: Distance push: fix the route before the roll plan
paragraphs: Skills affect the equipment you can acquire or fit, while the drive still depends on the car you assembled. Confirm that fuel and handling suit your planned attempt. Only then decide whether another support slot addresses a combat problem on that route.

If the route ends with fuel remaining but the car cannot survive contact, an owned additional weapon may justify capacity. If the tank empties first, more weapon capacity alone does not extend it. Let the failure identify the next experiment instead of buying every branch evenly.

subsections.heading: Established garage: inspect the Gold Roll path
paragraphs: Once the basic car and useful early upgrades are covered, review Unlock Gold Roll and the connected Gold Roll nodes. Read both the prerequisite and the effect before buying. A node name by itself does not establish its exact interval, reward pool or cost.

Check the total path you must buy rather than budgeting for the final tooltip alone. Keep ordinary equipment purchases available while working toward it. A longer-term upgrade is easier to evaluate when it does not prevent you from making another productive drive.

sections.heading: Read the skill tree before spending

steps.heading: Open SKILLS and find the relevant branch
steps.description: Choose the outcome you need first: better rolling, more support room or gold-roll progression. Look for the named node and inspect its current tooltip.

steps.heading: Trace the prerequisite path
steps.description: Check earlier ranks or other unlock conditions shown by the interface. A visible later node is not necessarily ready to buy.

steps.heading: Compare the whole purchase with your Cash
steps.description: Include any prerequisite purchases and the vehicle part you still need. Save toward a specific unlock instead of dividing your balance between unrelated branches.

steps.heading: Confirm what changed after purchase
steps.description: For capacity, inspect the builder counter. For Luck or Gold Roll, read the new unlocked state and the roll interface. A single ordinary roll cannot demonstrate the long-term effect of a luck upgrade.

paragraphs: Purchased Skills remain part of progression between normal runs. That makes them different from moving one weapon to another mounting point. It does not establish a promise about every future update or a particular reset feature, so inspect any reset prompt before confirming it.

Avoid comparing a Robux luck offer with a Cash skill as though they are the same purchase. Read which currency the interface requests and which benefit it describes. The useful decision is what your next earned Cash should solve, not whether an unrelated shop offer has a similar name.

sections.heading: Common skill purchase mistakes
bullets: Buying support capacity before owning a second piece you want to mount. Check inventory first.
Expecting Luck to guarantee a rare result on the next roll. Evaluate the unlocked effect, not one lucky or unlucky pull.
Budgeting only for a final node while ignoring prerequisites on the path.
Spending the entire balance on a lasting upgrade when the current car still lacks a usable movement part.
Copying an old price table instead of reading the current tooltip before purchase.
paragraphs: A short purchase note is enough: record the node, its displayed effect and why it solves your next problem. After a few drives, compare whether that problem remains. This habit keeps the upgrade route understandable even as your inventory and the game interface change.

faq.answer: Buy it when the support limit blocks equipment you already own and want to use. Check the builder counter and make sure your layout has a useful mounting position.

hero.heading: How to Get Cash Fast in Build and Kill Zombies
hero.lead: Earn Cash through driving distance and zombie kills, then compare the payout with the full time spent on each run. A repeatable car and a clear spending plan help you learn which setup earns more in your own sessions.

sections.heading: Separate repeatable Cash from one-time rewards
paragraphs: The normal repeatable earning loop is driving and fighting zombies. Distance and kills both contribute to the result, so use the Cash shown after a drive when comparing cars. Best distance is useful progression information, but it is not the same as the amount earned during an entire play session.

Codes can add Cash or equipment when a reported offer is still available and your account meets its requirements. Treat those claims as a separate starting bonus. They do not repeat every drive, and event currencies such as Crypt Tokens should not be counted as Cash.

sections.heading: A practical farming loop for a new garage

steps.heading: Establish one dependable car
steps.description: Build a compact moving setup before chasing a rare part. Use the car you can drive now, then inspect what actually stops the attempt.

steps.heading: Add a useful first weapon
steps.description: Mount owned equipment where it reaches zombies. A weapon hidden behind the body does not help you compare the value of combat income.

steps.heading: Repeat a familiar drive
steps.description: Use a route and driving approach you can reproduce. Learn its turns and the point where your current setup struggles, instead of changing destinations every attempt.

steps.heading: Record payout and full time
steps.description: Start timing before the drive preparation you want to compare and stop when you are ready for the next run. Include time spent returning and making required adjustments.

steps.heading: Buy or move one thing
steps.description: Address the repeated limitation, then compare several similar attempts. Keep the improvement only if its benefit survives more than one unusually good run.

paragraphs: Start with a few ordinary drives before spending the entire balance. If you cannot explain why the last car stopped, a new purchase gives you another unknown. A short run that teaches you the bottleneck can be more useful than repeatedly forcing the same failing record attempt.

Avoid unnecessary rebuilding between every drive. Once a basic layout works, preserve it long enough to form a comparison. When you change the engine, fuel and weapon at once, the next payout cannot show which decision helped.

sections.heading: Improve the constraint that keeps returning

subsections.heading: Fuel keeps ending the attempt
paragraphs: Inspect fuel before buying another weapon. An otherwise capable car gains little from extra equipment if the next drive ends at the same fuel limit. Compare a fuel change on a familiar run and check whether the longer drive adds enough Cash to justify the extra time.

subsections.heading: The car travels but kills poorly
paragraphs: Check contact and firing direction before rolling for replacements. A free placement change is a useful first experiment. If the mount now reaches targets but coverage is still limited, consider an additional owned weapon and inspect the support capacity you would need.

subsections.heading: Rebuilds and handling consume the session
paragraphs: Simplify the frame and remove additions that do not solve a specific problem. Count rebuilding and return time in your notes. A car with a larger single payout may still be less convenient if each attempt requires much more setup.

subsections.heading: You have a dependable earning baseline
paragraphs: Set aside Cash for the next useful offer or Skill rather than buying every roll. Luck supports future equipment progression; More Support matters when a limit blocks an owned mount. Neither choice should be assigned a guaranteed Cash return without results from your own sessions.

sections.heading: Keep a simple run log
sections.intro: Copy this checklist into your notes. Use actual results; there is no official earnings prediction hidden in this method. Compare a small group of runs under similar conditions and keep unusual bonuses separate.

table.caption: Fields to record for each attempt
rows: A short name and the one change since the previous setup
The displayed run payout, excluding separate code claims
Drive plus the preparation and return time you are comparing
Distance reached and what ended or limited the attempt
Keep it, revert it or test one specific adjustment

paragraphs: For a manual comparison, divide your observed Cash by the total minutes you recorded. This is a personal tracking calculation, not the game payout formula. For example, use the same start and finish points for timing both cars; comparing drive time for one with full session time for the other would mislead you.

Look for repeatability across several attempts. If a new setup has one excellent run followed by repeated failures, investigate the failures before declaring it the better farmer. Record route changes or exceptional rewards rather than quietly including them in the average.

Spend toward a named improvement and stop when it solves the issue you measured. Continuing to roll after obtaining a useful part can use the Cash you needed to buy the next offer. A clear stopping point keeps farming tied to progression rather than to endless purchases.

faq.question: What is the repeatable way to earn Cash?
faq.answer: Drive and fight zombies with a car you can use consistently. Compare the displayed payout and full time per attempt, then improve the limitation that repeatedly ends your runs.

faq.question: Is the farthest run always the best Cash farm?
faq.answer: Compare actual Cash and total session time. Distance is only one contributor, and rebuilding or unreliable attempts can change which setup is more useful for repeated play.

faq.question: Should I buy weapons or fuel first?
faq.answer: Use the repeated failure: fuel when the tank stops the attempt, weapon placement when targets pass untouched, and handling when the car cannot drive consistently. Test one change before another purchase.

faq.question: Can codes replace Cash farming?
faq.answer: Codes can provide a limited bonus when available. Check the current report and account requirements, then separate those claims from recurring driving income in your notes.

faq.question: Is there a fixed Cash-per-minute target?
faq.answer: No target is promised here. Use the payout and elapsed time from your own sessions to compare available cars. Keep event rewards, code claims and different timing methods separate.
